```{r}
#| include: false
library(grid)

draw_person <- function(x, y, s = 0.04, col = "#334155") {
  grid.circle(x, y + s * 0.45, r = s * 0.30,
              gp = gpar(fill = col, col = NA))
  tx <- c(x - s * 0.48, x + s * 0.48, x + s * 0.34, x - s * 0.34)
  ty <- c(y - s * 0.45, y - s * 0.45, y + s * 0.12, y + s * 0.12)
  grid.polygon(tx, ty, gp = gpar(fill = col, col = NA))
}
```

## Motivation

We have been classifying democracies based on how they distribute power

- Type of government $\rightarrow$ Parliamentary vs. Presidential
- Electoral system $\rightarrow$ Majoritarian vs. Proportional
- Party system $\rightarrow$ Two-party vs. Multiparty

. . . 

Today, we focus on constraints on executive power

- [Veto players]{.alert} $\Leftrightarrow$ [Checks and balances]{.alert}





## Our Plan for Today

[Veto players]{.alert} $\rightarrow$ actors whose agreement is necessary to change the status quo

- [Federalism]{.alert} $\rightarrow$ power division between national and sub-national units
- [Bicameralism]{.alert} $\rightarrow$ two legislative chambers
- [Constitutionalism]{.alert} $\rightarrow$ overarching rules and principles in the constitution (we won't cover it, see textbook)


# Veto Player Theory {.section}

## Veto Player Theory

[Institutional]{.alert} veto players $\rightarrow$ generated by a country's constitution

- E.g., USA $\rightarrow$ the president, House, and Senate can block changes to the status quo
- They are stable over time

. . . 

[Partisan]{.alert} veto players $\rightarrow$ generated by political competition

- E.g., minority parties in govt coalition $\rightarrow$ can block legislation
- Change over elections

. . . 

According to VPT, federalism, bicameralism, and constitutionalism can be seen as part of the same system of veto players/checks and balances

- They all serve to check and constrain executive decisions

# Federalism {.section}

## Federalism in Structure

A country is federal if it satisfies three criteria:

- [Geopolitical division]{.alert} $\rightarrow$ mutually exclusive regional governments that are recognized in the constitution and cannot be unilaterally abolished by the government

- [Independence]{.alert} $\rightarrow$ regional and national governments must have independent bases of authority (i.e., independent elections)

- [Direct governance]{.alert} $\rightarrow$ levels of government have independent authority over different policy areas, as written in the constitution


## Congruent vs. Incongruent Federalism

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-width: 8.8
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| out-width: "800px"
#| out-height: "320px"

grid.newpage()

draw_unit_grid <- function(cx, cy, cols_mat, title_txt) {
  grid.text(title_txt, cx, 0.90, gp = gpar(fontsize = 13, fontface = "bold", col = "#0F172A"))
  uw <- 0.11; uh <- 0.28; gap <- 0.012
  for (r in 1:2) {
    for (c in 1:3) {
      ux <- cx + (c - 2) * (uw + gap)
      uy <- cy + (1.5 - r) * (uh + gap)
      fill_c <- cols_mat[r, c]
      grid.roundrect(ux, uy, width = uw, height = uh, r = unit(0.015, "snpc"),
                     gp = gpar(fill = "#F8FAFC", col = "#64748B", lwd = 1.6))
      if (length(fill_c) == 1 && fill_c == "MIX") {
        draw_person(ux - 0.028, uy, s = 0.032, col = "#2563EB")
        draw_person(ux,         uy, s = 0.032, col = "#F59E0B")
        draw_person(ux + 0.028, uy, s = 0.032, col = "#16A34A")
      } else {
        draw_person(ux - 0.028, uy, s = 0.032, col = fill_c)
        draw_person(ux,         uy, s = 0.032, col = fill_c)
        draw_person(ux + 0.028, uy, s = 0.032, col = fill_c)
      }
    }
  }
}

mix_mat <- matrix("MIX", nrow = 2, ncol = 3)
inc_mat <- matrix(c("#2563EB", "#F59E0B", "#F59E0B",
                    "#2563EB", "#16A34A", "#F59E0B"), nrow = 2, ncol = 3, byrow = TRUE)

draw_unit_grid(0.26, 0.45, mix_mat, "Congruent (e.g., US, Brazil)")
draw_unit_grid(0.74, 0.45, inc_mat, "Incongruent (e.g., Switzerland)")
```


:::{.nonincremental}
- [Congruent]{.alert} federalism $\rightarrow$ units have similar demographic characteristics
    - E.g., USA, Brazil, Germany
- [Incongruent]{.alert} federalism $\rightarrow$ different groups are geographically concentrated
    - E.g., Swiss cantons, Belgian regions, Nigerian states
:::

## Symmetric vs. Asymmetric Federalism

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-width: 8.8
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| out-width: "800px"
#| out-height: "320px"

grid.newpage()

draw_sym_panel <- function(cx, cy, powers, cols, title_txt) {
  grid.text(title_txt, cx, 0.90, gp = gpar(fontsize = 13, fontface = "bold", col = "#0F172A"))
  grid.roundrect(cx, 0.74, width = 0.34, height = 0.09, r = unit(0.015, "snpc"),
                 gp = gpar(fill = "#1E293B", col = NA))
  grid.text("Center", cx, 0.74, gp = gpar(fontsize = 10, fontface = "bold", col = "#FFFFFF"))
  
  n <- 4
  xs <- seq(cx - 0.135, cx + 0.135, length.out = n)
  for (i in 1:n) {
    bh <- powers[i]
    grid.roundrect(xs[i], 0.20 + bh/2, width = 0.072, height = bh, r = unit(0.012, "snpc"),
                   gp = gpar(fill = cols[i], col = "#0F172A", lwd = 1.2))
  }
}

draw_sym_panel(0.26, 0.45, rep(0.24, 4), rep("#93C5FD", 4), "Symmetric (e.g., US)")
draw_sym_panel(0.74, 0.45, c(0.20, 0.40, 0.20, 0.20), c("#93C5FD", "#2563EB", "#93C5FD", "#93C5FD"), "Asymmetric (e.g., Canada)")
```

:::{.nonincremental}
- [Symmetric]{.alert} federalism $\rightarrow$ units have equal powers relative to the central govt
- [Asymmetric]{.alert} federalism $\rightarrow$ some units have more extensive powers than others
:::

## Federalism in Practice: (De)Centralization

- A federal vs. unitary state is a formal difference
- In practice, powers can be very unbalanced in a federal state
- E.g., units can have formal authority but little capacity to raise taxes
- Having fiscal resources is crucial for units to actually govern
- Revenue [centralization]{.alert} indicates how much power is effectively distributed

:::{.fragment}
Centralization = % Total taxes collected by the central government 
:::

## Why Federalism?

::::{.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}
[Coming-together]{.alert} explanation $\rightarrow$ "bottom-up"

- Sovereign polities voluntarily agree to pool resources
- Achieve collective goals: collective security, a common currency, a trade area
- E.g., Australia, Switzerland, United States
:::
:::{.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-width: 4.6
#| fig-height: 3.8
#| out-width: "420px"
#| out-height: "340px"

grid.newpage()
arr <- arrow(angle = 22, length = unit(0.11, "inches"), ends = "last", type = "closed")
ux <- c(0.18, 0.50, 0.82)
for (x in ux) {
  grid.roundrect(x, 0.22, width = 0.20, height = 0.16, r = unit(0.02, "snpc"),
                 gp = gpar(fill = "#DBEAFE", col = "#2563EB", lwd = 2))
  grid.lines(c(x, 0.50 + (x - 0.50)*0.25), c(0.32, 0.62), arrow = arr,
             gp = gpar(col = "#2563EB", fill = "#2563EB", lwd = 2.5))
}
grid.roundrect(0.50, 0.75, width = 0.44, height = 0.18, r = unit(0.025, "snpc"),
               gp = gpar(fill = "#1E293B", col = NA))
grid.text("Federal Union", 0.50, 0.75, gp = gpar(fontsize = 12, fontface = "bold", col = "#FFFFFF"))
```
:::
::::

## Why Federalism?

::::{.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}
[Holding-together]{.alert} explanation $\rightarrow$ "top-down"

- Central government decentralizes power to subnational governments
- Appease local communities (regions, ethnicities) that threaten secession
- E.g., Belgium, India, Spain, United Kingdom
- Tends to produce both incongruent and asymmetric federalism
:::
:::{.column width="50%"}

## Federalism: Potential Advantages

```{r}

grid.newpage()
arr <- arrow(angle = 20, length = unit(0.09, "inches"), ends = "both", type = "closed")

cx1 <- 0.26
grid.text("Single Unit", cx1, 0.90, gp = gpar(fontsize = 13, fontface = "bold", col = "#0F172A"))
grid.roundrect(cx1, 0.42, width = 0.38, height = 0.68, r = unit(0.02, "snpc"),
```

# Bicameralism {.section}

## What Is Bicameralism?

Number of legislative assemblies in a country

- [Unicameral]{.alert} legislature $\rightarrow$ single assembly
- [Bicameral]{.alert} legislature $\rightarrow$ two distinct assemblies

. . . 

Why does this matter?

- In bicameral systems, assemblies can typically veto each other
- This generates [strategic incentives]{.alert} for legislators

## Strategic Possibilities in Bicameralism

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-width: 8.4
#| fig-height: 3.4
#| out-width: "760px"
#| out-height: "300px"

grid.newpage()
arr <- arrow(angle = 20, length = unit(0.10, "inches"), ends = "last", type = "closed")

grid.roundrect(0.16, 0.50, width = 0.20, height = 0.44, r = unit(0.02, "snpc"),
               gp = gpar(fill = "#EFF6FF", col = "#2563EB", lwd = 2))
grid.text("Lower\nChamber", 0.16, 0.50, gp = gpar(fontsize = 11, fontface = "bold", col = "#1E40AF"))

grid.roundrect(0.36, 0.50, width = 0.07, height = 0.18, r = unit(0.01, "snpc"),
               gp = gpar(fill = "#FFFFFF", col = "#475569", lwd = 1.8))
grid.text("Bill", 0.36, 0.50, gp = gpar(fontsize = 9, fontface = "bold", col = "#334155"))

grid.lines(c(0.27, 0.32), c(0.50, 0.50), arrow = arr, gp = gpar(col = "#475569", fill = "#475569", lwd = 2))
grid.lines(c(0.40, 0.47), c(0.50, 0.50), arrow = arr, gp = gpar(col = "#475569", fill = "#475569", lwd = 2))

grid.roundrect(0.58, 0.50, width = 0.20, height = 0.44, r = unit(0.02, "snpc"),
               gp = gpar(fill = "#F8FAFC", col = "#1E293B", lwd = 2))
grid.text("Upper\nChamber", 0.58, 0.50, gp = gpar(fontsize = 11, fontface = "bold", col = "#0F172A"))

ys_out <- c(0.76, 0.50, 0.24)
cols_out <- c("#16A34A", "#D97706", "#DC2626")
bg_out   <- c("#F0FDF4", "#FFFBEB", "#FEF2F2")
txt_out  <- c("Approve", "Delay", "Veto")

for (i in 1:3) {
  grid.lines(c(0.69, 0.77), c(0.50 + (ys_out[i]-0.50)*0.4, ys_out[i]), arrow = arr,
             gp = gpar(col = cols_out[i], fill = cols_out[i], lwd = 2.2))
  grid.roundrect(0.87, ys_out[i], width = 0.16, height = 0.15, r = unit(0.02, "snpc"),
                 gp = gpar(fill = bg_out[i], col = cols_out[i], lwd = 1.8))
  grid.text(txt_out[i], 0.87, ys_out[i], gp = gpar(fontsize = 10.5, fontface = "bold", col = cols_out[i]))
}
```

- Upper chamber can credibly threaten to delay or veto a bill
- Lower chamber legislators adapt to the threat 
    - Produce bills that are likely to pass
    - Vote "irresponsibly" knowing the upper chamber will veto


## Congruent vs. Incongruent Bicameralism

- [Congruent]{.alert} bicameralism $\rightarrow$ the two chambers have similar political composition

- [Incongruent]{.alert} bicameralism $\rightarrow$ the two chambers have different political composition

- This may arise by institutional design

- Different election rules $\rightarrow$ methods or suffrage

- Different representation goals $\rightarrow$ voters vs. territories


## Different Electoral Rules


The lower chamber is directly elected by universal suffrage. This is not necessarily the case for the upper chamber.

. . . 

Differences include:

- Restricted suffrage $\rightarrow$ different voting age
    - E.g., Italian Senate until 2020 ($\geq$ 25 y.o.)

- Indirect election $\rightarrow$ elected by local or regional bodies
    - E.g., Argentina until 1994 (provincial legislatures)

- Appointment $\rightarrow$ by regional or national government
    - E.g., German Bundesrat (state govts)

- Heredity $\rightarrow$ some monarchies
    - E.g., UK House of Lords until 1999


## Different Representation Goals

The lower chamber is supposed to represent all citizens equally. This is not necessarily the case for the upper chamber.

. . . 

Differences include:

- Represent some sectors of society 
    - E.g., Irish senators (civil society "panels")

- Ensure representation of ethnic or linguistic groups  
    - E.g., Belgian senators (linguistic regions' parliaments)

- Ensure equal representation of regions $\rightarrow$ federal systems
    - E.g., US and Mexican Senates (fixed members per state)

- Regional representation $\implies$ [malapportionment]{.alert}
    - Regions with few inhabitants are **overrepresented**

## Malapportionment: An Illustration

## Symmetric vs. Asymmetric Bicameralism

- [Symmetric]{.alert} bicameralism $\rightarrow$ the two chambers have (nearly) equal powers 
    - The agreement of both chambers is needed to enact a law

- [Asymmetric]{.alert} bicameralism $\rightarrow$ the two chambers have unequal powers
    - The lower chamber is the one with more power

## Two Dimensions of Bicameralism

- Symmetric and incongruent bicameralism is stronger
- Strong chambers with different preferences can keep each other in check

# Summing Up {.section}


## What We Learned

- The configuration of veto players is a key institutional feature of a country

- Veto players determine how hard it is to change the political status quo 

- What matters: not just their number, but how different their preferences are

:::{.fragment}

```{r}
grid.lines(c(0.86, 0.86), c(0.36, 0.50), gp = gpar(col = "#DC2626", lwd = 3.5, lineend = "round"))
```
:::


## Final Remarks

- Systems with many veto players are essentially designed to ensure broad agreement exists for political changes

- Whether policy stability or status quo bias is good or bad is unclear

- The cost of many heterogeneous players can be excessive policy stability, status quo bias, or "gridlock"

- On the other hand, paraphrasing Lijphart: "If you don't like ethnic gridlock, try ethnic conflict"

- Which leads us to our final lecture (next week)
